title: Building and Running a Portfolio
intro: Theory says hold a diversified portfolio at a level of risk you can live with. This page turns that into decisions: how to split money between stocks, bonds and cash, how to put money in, when to rebalance, how to place assets in accounts, and how to turn a portfolio into income in retirement without running out.

blocks.text: Start from goals

Write down each goal with an amount and a date: an emergency fund now, a house deposit in four years, retirement in thirty. Each goal gets its own time horizon and so its own mix. Money for the next few years should not depend on the stock market; money for decades from now can ride out crashes, because there is time to recover and to keep buying cheaply.
Asset allocation

The split between asset classes explains most of the variation in a diversified portfolio's returns over time (Brinson, Hood and Beebower 1986, often over-quoted, but the point stands): for a typical investor, choosing 80/20 instead of 40/60 matters far more than which funds fill each slice. Three things set the right mix:

items: Ability to take risk: time horizon, job stability, other income and assets. A young worker with a stable salary has a large 'bond-like' asset in future earnings and can hold more stocks.
Willingness to take risk: how you will behave in a 40% fall. A portfolio you abandon in a crash is worse than a milder one you hold.
Need to take risk: if your goals are met with low risk, extra risk adds little.
Rules of thumb: 'age in bonds' (a 30-year-old holds 30% bonds) or '110 minus age in stocks'. Crude, but they encode the idea of reducing risk as the horizon shortens.
Classic 60/40: 60% stocks, 40% bonds; the reference balanced portfolio, which lost about 17% in 2022 when both fell.
Target-date funds apply a glide path automatically.

Home bias: investors everywhere overweight their own country. US stocks are over 60% of global stock market value; a UK investor holding mostly UK stocks is betting on 3 to 4% of the world. Holding a large share abroad diversifies country, currency and sector risk.

blocks.text: Getting money in: lump sum or dollar-cost averaging

Dollar-cost averaging (DCA) invests a fixed amount at regular intervals. For saving from each paycheck it is simply how investing happens, and it buys more shares when prices are low. With a lump sum already in hand the question is different. Because markets rise more often than they fall, investing at once has beaten spreading it over 6 to 12 months about two-thirds of the time historically (Vanguard studies across the US, UK and Australia). DCA reduces regret if the market drops right after you invest, at the cost of lower expected wealth. If the fear of a bad start would stop you investing at all, a short DCA schedule is a reasonable compromise.

Market timing (moving in and out based on forecasts) has a poor record. Missing a handful of the best days, which tend to cluster near the worst ones, cuts long-run returns sharply. 'Time in the market beats timing the market' is a cliché because the data support it.
Rebalancing

Over time winners grow and the portfolio drifts away from its target, usually toward more stocks and more risk. Rebalancing sells some of what has risen and buys what has lagged, restoring the target. Its main purpose is to control risk; any return bonus from 'buying low and selling high' is modest and not guaranteed.

items: Calendar: once or twice a year.
Threshold: when an asset class drifts more than, say, 5 percentage points (or 20% of its target) from target.
Use cash flows first: direct new contributions or withdrawals to the underweight asset, avoiding sales and taxes.
Rebalance inside tax-advantaged accounts where possible, since sales there are untaxed.

blocks.text: Asset location

With both taxable and tax-advantaged accounts, put the least tax-efficient assets where they are sheltered. In US terms: taxable bonds, REITs and high-turnover funds go in IRAs and 401(k)s; broad stock index funds (low dividends, few gains distributions, eligible for lower long-term rates and the foreign tax credit) go in taxable accounts; the assets with the highest expected growth are best in Roth accounts. The gain is typically a few tenths of a percent a year: small, free and compounding.
Spending a portfolio: withdrawal rates

William Bengen (1994) looked at US history and asked how much a retiree could withdraw in the first year, then raise each year with inflation, without running out in 30 years, holding 50 to 75% stocks. The worst historical case allowed about 4% of the starting balance: the 4% rule. The Trinity study (Cooley, Hubbard and Walz, 1998) found similar results. Later work points out that the 4% rule relied on US returns, which were among the world's best, and on 30 years; for longer retirements, lower expected returns or other countries' histories, 3 to 3.5% has been safer. Flexible rules that cut spending after bad years (Guyton-Klinger guardrails, percentage-of-portfolio rules) allow higher average spending.
Sequence-of-returns risk

While you save, the order of returns doesn't matter for the final balance if you invest once and never add. While you withdraw, it matters a great deal: losses early in retirement force you to sell more shares at low prices, and those shares can't recover. The plot below applies the same 30 yearly returns in two orders. Its bad stretch (three years of −15% real, a 39% loss) is harsher than anything in Bengen's US data, so it runs out even at 4%; it is a stress test, not a forecast.

blocks.text: Both orders have the same compound average return, and with no withdrawals they would end at exactly the same place. With withdrawals, three bad years at the start can leave a much smaller balance, or nothing at all than the same three bad years at the end. Defenses: a lower initial withdrawal rate, a few years of spending in bonds or cash, flexible spending, delaying retirement or claiming a larger government pension later (in the US, delaying Social Security from 62 to 70 raises the benefit by roughly 75%), and annuities that pay for life.
Monte Carlo simulation

A Monte Carlo plan generates thousands of random return sequences from assumed means, volatilities and correlations, and reports the share in which the money lasts. It is only as good as its assumptions: normal returns understate crashes, and a '90% success rate' says nothing about how bad the 10% is or how you would adjust along the way. Use it to compare choices, not to promise outcomes.
An investment policy statement

Write a one-page plan when markets are calm: goals, target allocation, the funds that fill each part, when you rebalance, how much you save, and what you will do in a crash (usually: nothing, or rebalance). Reading it in a panic is the cheapest risk management there is.
Practice

blocks.title: Rebalancing
blocks.text: A \$100,000 portfolio targets 60% stocks and 40% bonds. After a year stocks have risen 25% and bonds 2%. What is the new mix, and what trade restores the target?
solution: Stocks: \$75,000; bonds: \$40,800; total \$115,800. Stocks are now 64.8%.
Target stocks: $0.6 \times 115800 = \$69{,}480$. Sell about \$5,520 of stocks and buy \$5,520 of bonds.

blocks.title: Withdrawal rate
blocks.text: You plan to spend \$48,000 a year from your portfolio in retirement, adjusting for inflation. How much do you need at a 4% withdrawal rate? At 3.3%?

blocks.title: Lump sum or DCA
blocks.text: You inherit \$60,000 and are deciding between investing it now in a 60/40 fund and investing \$5,000 a month for a year. Expected returns are 6% a year on the fund and 4% on cash. Roughly how much expected return do you give up by spreading it out?
solution: On average half the money sits in cash for about six months, earning 2% a year less than the fund: roughly $60000 \times 0.5 \times 0.02 \approx \$600$ (about \$550 if the first instalment goes in at once). Small in expectation; the real difference is in the spread of outcomes and how you would feel about each.
